actions.justification: Mandatory first step - must assess for active bleeding to determine urgency and guide transfusion decisions.
Mandatory - hemodynamic status assessment is critical to determine if patient is stable or requires urgent intervention.
Mandatory - CBC is required to determine hemoglobin level and guide transfusion threshold decisions.
Mandatory action — must be completed within 60 minutes. Type and screen is essential before any blood product administration to identify blood type and detect antibodies, ensuring safe transfusion.
Mandatory action — must be completed within 60 minutes. Reviewing prior transfusion history identifies previous reactions, alloantibodies, and guides safe blood product selection.

Optional but clinically indicated — assessing symptoms of anemia (fatigue, dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia) will help determine whether a liberal or restrictive transfusion threshold is appropriate for this patient.

Patient is hemodynamically stable (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%) with no signs of active hemorrhage. Evidence-based guidelines support a restrictive transfusion threshold (Hb <7-8 g/dL) in stable patients to minimize transfusion-related risks while awaiting CBC results.
Acetaminophen is a standard pre-transfusion medication to reduce febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions if transfusion is anticipated based on CBC results.
Diphenhydramine is a standard pre-transfusion antihistamine premedication to reduce allergic transfusion reactions if transfusion is anticipated.
Maintaining IV access is essential for ongoing fluid or blood product administration pending CBC results, ensuring rapid response capability if transfusion is needed.
Normothermia maintenance is critical in transfusion management to prevent coagulopathy and hypothermia-related complications while awaiting CBC results.
Patient is stable but requires ongoing serial vital sign monitoring every 15 minutes to detect any hemodynamic changes while awaiting CBC results and transfusion decision-making.
Coagulation status monitoring is important in the context of potential transfusion therapy to guide product selection and identify coagulopathy before initiating transfusion.

Tranexamic acid may be indicated if active bleeding is present or suspected; given the transfusion context and pending labs, this is a reasonable proactive measure to reduce fibrinolysis if bleeding is confirmed.
Reticulocyte count helps characterize the type of anemia (hypoproliferative vs. hemolytic) to guide transfusion and treatment decisions while CBC is pending.
Iron studies will help identify iron deficiency anemia vs. anemia of chronic disease, informing both transfusion thresholds and adjunctive treatment planning.
Direct antiglobulin test (DAT) is important to rule out hemolytic anemia or transfusion reaction, which is critical in a patient with transfusion history.

Patient has been in the department for 85 minutes with labs still pending. Serial hemodynamic reassessment is warranted to detect any deterioration and guide transfusion decisions once CBC results return.
CBC is pending; reassessing hemoglobin level is critical to determine if transfusion thresholds have been reached and to guide further management decisions.

With coagulation monitoring ongoing and transfusion workup in progress, TEG provides real-time assessment of clot formation and can guide component therapy decisions (e.g., FFP, platelets, cryoprecipitate) if active coagulopathy is suspected.
Blood bank workup should be sent to facilitate crossmatching and evaluate for any transfusion reactions or compatibility issues, supporting safe transfusion planning once CBC results return.
With hemodynamic stability and pending CBC, prepare to transfuse if hemoglobin falls below 8 g/dL per standard restrictive transfusion threshold guidelines for this patient population.

With CBC pending at 110 minutes, establishing the transfusion threshold of Hb <7 g/dL is appropriate for a stable patient, consistent with restrictive transfusion strategy already initiated. This prepares the team to act once results return.
If blood products are being transfused, calcium gluconate should be given to counteract citrate-induced hypocalcemia, which can cause cardiac dysfunction during transfusion.
